## Normative Language Convention

Requirements in this document use the normative language convention defined in [GUID-SEC-AI-VISION-0.9.01 §Normative Language Convention](../../guidance/security/GUID-SEC-AI-VISION-0.9.01.md): **SHALL** = mandatory; **SHOULD** = strongly recommended (deviation requires documented justification); **MAY** = optional.

## Executive Summary

Artificial Intelligence is no longer a future investment for Gainwell Technologies — it is a present operational reality embedded in claims adjudication, care management, fraud detection, and population health analytics. Realizing the full value of these AI investments requires operating them with confidence: with clear visibility into their security posture, demonstrable control over their risks, and the governance evidence that clients and regulators increasingly expect.

**AI Security Posture Management (AI SPM)** is the emerging discipline — and corresponding class of tooling — that provides this confidence. AI SPM delivers continuous, automated visibility into the security posture of AI and ML systems: their models, training data, inference pipelines, APIs, governance controls, and regulatory compliance state.

This white paper establishes the authoritative **capability requirements and business requirements** for an AI SPM capability at Gainwell. These requirements draw from the **NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)**, **NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0**, **NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5**, **NIST SP 800-218A** (Secure Software Development for AI), **MITRE ATLAS**, **OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025**, and relevant IETF standards. They are technology-agnostic and structured to define the capability independent of any specific implementation approach.

### Key Business Drivers

| Driver | Description |
|---|---|
| **Regulatory Exposure** | Federal and state customers increasingly require documented AI risk management aligned to NIST AI RMF and emerging AI governance mandates |
| **Operational Risk** | AI systems operating without security visibility represent unquantified, unmitigated material risk |
| **Threat Landscape Evolution** | Adversarial ML attacks (prompt injection, model inversion, data poisoning) are actively exploited; traditional SIEM/SOAR tooling does not detect them |
| **Audit Readiness** | HIPAA, state Medicaid agreements, and emerging AI-specific audit requirements demand evidence of security controls across the AI lifecycle |
| **Supply Chain Risk** | Dependency on third-party models, datasets, and AI platforms introduces provenance and integrity risks not addressed by current tooling |
| **Zero Trust Extension** | The enterprise Zero Trust architecture must extend identity, policy enforcement, and continuous verification to AI inference endpoints and model serving APIs |

### 1.1 What AI SPM Uniquely Addresses

AI and ML systems have characteristics that existing security tooling was not designed to handle. This is an industry-wide maturity challenge — not unique to Gainwell — and it is the reason AI Security Posture Management has emerged as a distinct discipline. AI SPM complements existing CSPM, SIEM, and GRC investments by addressing the following AI-specific security characteristics:

- **Models are probabilistic and opaque.** Behavior cannot be fully validated through traditional test coverage alone, requiring AI-specific assessment approaches.
- **Training data is itself an attack surface.** Poisoned data can influence model behavior in ways that are difficult to detect through standard monitoring.
- **Inference APIs can expose model internals.** Model inversion and membership inference techniques can extract information about training data through production APIs.
- **Prompt injection is a novel attack class.** Large Language Models (LLMs) accept natural language instructions that can be crafted to override intended system behavior.
- **Model supply chains introduce unique risk.** Pre-trained foundation models from third parties may carry vulnerabilities, unverified provenance, or unexpected behaviors.
- **AI governance benefits significantly from automation.** Fairness assessments, explainability mechanisms, and accountability records are often managed manually today; AI SPM enables continuous evidence collection and reduces audit preparation burden.

The following table illustrates where AI SPM extends and complements existing security capabilities:

| Security Domain | Traditional Tooling | AI SPM Capability |
|---|---|---|
| Asset Inventory | CMDB, cloud discovery | AI model registry, dataset catalog, pipeline discovery |
| Vulnerability Management | CVE scanning, patch management | Adversarial robustness assessment, model card validation |
| Configuration Security | CIS benchmarks, CSPM | AI platform security baselines, MLOps pipeline hardening |
| Data Security | DLP, DSPM | Training data lineage, de-identification verification, inference data controls |
| Identity & Access | IAM, PAM | Model API authentication, inference service identity, feature store access |
| Threat Detection | SIEM, EDR | Adversarial input detection, prompt injection monitoring, model drift alerting |
| Incident Response | SOAR playbooks | AI-specific IR playbooks (model rollback, dataset quarantine) |
| Compliance | GRC platforms | NIST AI RMF mapping, automated AI audit evidence collection |

### 1.2 Regulatory and Standards Landscape

The following authoritative sources directly inform the capability requirements in this document:

| Standard / Framework | Relevance to AI SPM |
|---|---|
| **NIST AI RMF 1.0** (2023) | Four-function framework (GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE) for AI risk management; primary structural basis for requirement domains |
| **NIST CSF 2.0** (2024) | Six-function framework (GOVERN, IDENTIFY, PROTECT, DETECT, RESPOND, RECOVER); maps AI SPM capabilities to enterprise security functions |
| **NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5** | Control catalog for federal systems; AI SPM must demonstrate control satisfaction for SA, SI, RA, CA, AU, and IR families |
| **NIST SP 800-218A** (2024) | Secure Software Development Framework applied to AI/ML: maps SSDF practices to AI-specific development concerns |
| **NIST SP 800-226** (2024) | Evaluation of bias detection and mitigation in AI systems; required for fairness and accountability posture |
| **NIST AI 100-1** (2023) | AI Risk Management Framework Foundations; defines trustworthy AI characteristics |
| **MITRE ATLAS™** | AI-specific adversarial threat taxonomy; maps AI SPM detections to known TTP catalog |
| **OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025)** | Top 10 LLM application vulnerabilities; AI SPM SHALL cover all 10 categories for LLM deployments |
| **ISO/IEC 42001:2023** | AI Management System standard; organizational context for AI SPM governance |
| **IETF RFC 2119** | Normative language definitions; inherited via [GUID-SEC-AI-VISION-0.9.01 §Normative Language Convention](../../guidance/security/GUID-SEC-AI-VISION-0.9.01.md) |
| **IETF RFC 9334** | Remote ATtestation procedureS (RATS) architecture; applicable to AI model and platform integrity attestation |
| **IETF RFC 8705** | OAuth 2.0 Mutual-TLS Client Authentication; applicable to AI API service-to-service authentication |
| ~~**Executive Order 14110**~~ _(Revoked)_ | Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of AI (2023). **Revoked by Executive Order 14179 (January 23, 2025).** AI-BOM obligations previously cited from §4.2(e) are now grounded in NIST SP 800-218A PW.4.1 and enterprise policy. No longer cited as an active normative authority in this document. |
| **HIPAA Security Rule** | PHI protections must extend to AI training data, inference inputs, and model outputs |

### 1.3 Scope

These requirements apply to **all AI and ML systems** that are:

- Developed internally by Gainwell engineering teams
- Procured as third-party AI services or models integrated into Gainwell solutions
- Operated on behalf of state and federal clients as part of Gainwell's managed services
- Used in internal operations where they process regulated data (PHI, PII) or make consequential decisions affecting individuals or Gainwell business operations

**In scope AI system types:**

- Supervised and unsupervised ML models (classification, regression, clustering, anomaly detection)
- Deep learning models (CNNs, RNNs, transformers)
- Large Language Models (LLMs) and Generative AI systems
- Natural Language Processing (NLP) pipelines
- Predictive analytics and decision support systems
- Computer vision systems
- Recommender systems and personalization engines
- Automated decision-making systems with regulatory impact

**Out of scope:**

- Traditional rule-based systems with no learned model components
- Pure statistical reporting with no inferential model

## 2. Capability Requirements

The capability requirements are organized across **nine functional domains** that collectively define the AI SPM capability. Each domain includes a statement of purpose, business requirements (BR), and technical/functional requirements (FR) mapped to authoritative standards.

> **Minimum Viable Capabilities:** Not all nine domains need to be active simultaneously to deliver business value. A minimum viable capability is defined as: asset discovery and inventory (Domain 1), identity and access enforcement (Domain 7), and metrics and reporting (Domain 9) — providing baseline visibility, access governance, and risk measurement from day one. Remaining domains are prioritized using the enterprise AI System Risk Classification defined in [GUID-SEC-AI-GOV-2.9.06](../../guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-GOV-2.9.06.MD), with High-risk AI systems receiving full capability coverage first. Sequencing and resourcing decisions are made through the enterprise AI governance process.

### Domain 1: AI Asset Discovery and Inventory Management

**Purpose:** Enable continuous, automated discovery and cataloging of all AI assets across the enterprise, including models, datasets, pipelines, APIs, and supporting infrastructure. Without authoritative inventory, no subsequent security posture management is possible.

**Alignment:** NIST AI RMF MAP 1.1, MAP 1.5 | NIST CSF 2.0 ID.AM | NIST SP 800-53 CM-8
page_texts.13:
[strategy/white-papers/security/GUID-SEC-AI-SPM-REQS-v1.md#business-requirements]

#### Business Requirements

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| BR-INV-001 | The enterprise SHALL maintain a comprehensive inventory of all deployed AI models, kept current on an ongoing basis, including model name, version, type, business owner, data classification, and deployment environment. |
| BR-INV-002 | The inventory SHALL capture the lineage of each model, including training datasets, pre-trained base models, fine-tuning datasets, and associated feature stores. |
| BR-INV-003 | The inventory SHALL include all AI-consuming APIs, inference endpoints, and AI-enabled SaaS integrations. |
| BR-INV-004 | The enterprise SHALL assign a designated AI System Owner and AI Risk Owner to every cataloged AI asset, as defined by the role and responsibility framework in [GUID-SEC-AI-GOV-2.9.06 §Role Definitions](../../guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-GOV-2.9.06.MD). |
| BR-INV-005 | AI assets SHALL be classified by risk tier (High, Moderate, Low) in accordance with the enterprise AI System Risk Classification defined in [GUID-SEC-AI-GOV-2.9.06 §AI System Risk Classification](../../guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-GOV-2.9.06.MD), based on decision impact, data sensitivity, regulatory scope, and population exposure. |

> **Risk Tier Reference**: AI system risk tier classification (High/Moderate/Low) used throughout this document is defined in [GUID-SEC-AI-GOV-2.9.06 §AI System Risk Classification](../../guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-GOV-2.9.06.MD). Finding severity ratings (Critical/High/Medium/Low/Informational) are distinct from system risk tier and refer to the severity of individual security findings.
page_texts.14:
[strategy/white-papers/security/GUID-SEC-AI-SPM-REQS-v1.md#functional-requirements]

#### Functional Requirements

| ID | Requirement | Standards Alignment |
|---|---|---|
| FR-INV-001 | The AI SPM tool SHALL provide automated discovery of deployed models and inference endpoints through integration with MLOps platforms (e.g., MLflow, SageMaker, Azure ML, Vertex AI) without requiring manual self-registration as the sole inventory mechanism. | NIST AI RMF MAP 1.1 |
| FR-INV-002 | The tool SHALL maintain a standardized model card for each discovered AI asset, capturing at minimum: model purpose, input/output schema, training data lineage, known limitations, risk classification, compliance scope, and deployment status. | NIST AI 100-1; ISO/IEC 42001 §6.1.2 |
| FR-INV-003 | The tool SHALL discover AI assets deployed outside registered channels, enabling teams to onboard these assets into the governance program. Unregistered AI assets detected in production or staging environments SHALL generate workflow requests for governance registration, routed to the AI System Owner designation process. | NIST CSF 2.0 ID.AM-3; NIST AI RMF GOVERN 6.1 |
| FR-INV-004 | The asset inventory SHALL be queryable via API and SHALL integrate with the enterprise CMDB for unified asset governance. | NIST SP 800-53 CM-8(2) |
| FR-INV-005 | The tool SHALL provide a real-time, role-based inventory dashboard with filtering by risk tier, business unit, compliance scope, and deployment environment. | NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC-01 |
| FR-INV-006 | The tool SHALL track model lifecycle state (development, staging, production, deprecated, decommissioned) and generate alerts on lifecycle transitions without corresponding security review. | NIST AI RMF MANAGE 4.1 |

### Domain 2: AI Configuration Security Assessment

**Purpose:** Evaluate the configuration of AI platforms, MLOps pipelines, model serving infrastructure, and AI-adjacent cloud resources against approved security baselines and hardening standards.

**Alignment:** NIST AI RMF MAP 2.1, MEASURE 2.5 | NIST CSF 2.0 PR.PS | NIST SP 800-53 CM-6, CM-7 | NIST SP 800-218A PW.4
page_texts.16:
[strategy/white-papers/security/GUID-SEC-AI-SPM-REQS-v1.md#business-requirements]

#### Business Requirements

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| BR-CFG-001 | All AI platform configurations SHALL be validated against enterprise-approved security baselines before production deployment and re-validated at defined intervals proportional to risk tier thereafter. |
| BR-CFG-002 | Configuration drift from approved baselines SHALL be detected, alerted, and tracked to remediation. |
| BR-CFG-003 | MLOps pipeline configurations SHALL enforce code signing, artifact verification, and least-privilege service accounts at all pipeline stages. |
| BR-CFG-004 | AI-specific infrastructure hardening baselines SHALL be maintained as living documents reviewed at minimum annually and upon major platform updates. |
page_texts.17:
[strategy/white-papers/security/GUID-SEC-AI-SPM-REQS-v1.md#functional-requirements]

#### Functional Requirements

| ID | Requirement | Standards Alignment |
|---|---|---|
| FR-CFG-001 | The AI SPM tool SHALL assess the security configuration of AI platform components (Jupyter environments, ML experiment tracking servers, model registries, feature stores, vector databases) against defined CIS or equivalent hardening benchmarks. | NIST SP 800-53 CM-6; NIST SP 800-218A PW.4 |
| FR-CFG-002 | The tool SHALL assess CI/CD pipeline configurations for AI workloads, including pipeline-as-code integrity, secret management posture, and approval gate enforcement. | NIST SP 800-218A PO.3, PW.1; NIST SP 800-53 SA-12 |
| FR-CFG-003 | The tool SHALL detect and alert on overly permissive IAM policies attached to AI service accounts, model serving roles, and inference endpoint identities. | NIST SP 800-53 AC-6; NIST CSF 2.0 PR.AA-05 |
| FR-CFG-004 | The tool SHALL assess container and Kubernetes configurations used to host AI workloads, including privileged container detection, network policy gaps, and secrets storage misconfigurations. | NIST SP 800-53 CM-7; NIST CSF 2.0 PR.PS-01 |
| FR-CFG-005 | Configuration assessments SHALL produce findings with severity ratings (Critical, High, Medium, Low, Informational) mapped to NIST SP 800-53 control identifiers. | NIST SP 800-53 CA-7; NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-01 |
| FR-CFG-006 | The tool SHALL support policy-as-code for configuration baselines, enabling version-controlled, peer-reviewed policy definitions integrated into the infrastructure CI/CD pipeline. | NIST SP 800-218A PO.3.2 |

### Domain 3: AI Model Risk and Integrity Assessment

**Purpose:** Evaluate the security posture of AI models themselves — including adversarial robustness, model integrity verification, supply chain provenance, and protection against model-level attacks (inversion, extraction, backdoor).

**Alignment:** NIST AI RMF MEASURE 2.1, MEASURE 2.5, MEASURE 2.6 | NIST SP 800-53 SI-7, SA-12 | MITRE ATLAS | OWASP LLM Top 10
page_texts.19:
[strategy/white-papers/security/GUID-SEC-AI-SPM-REQS-v1.md#business-requirements]

#### Business Requirements

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| BR-MDL-001 | Production AI models SHALL undergo adversarial robustness assessment prior to deployment and following any significant retraining. Assessment rigor SHALL be proportional to risk tier: High-risk systems SHALL complete full adversarial robustness assessment; Moderate-risk systems SHOULD complete adversarial testing; Low-risk systems MAY substitute documented input validation and anomaly detection controls. This tiering aligns to [GUID-SEC-AI-MODEL-2.9.02](../../guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-MODEL-2.9.02.md). |
| BR-MDL-002 | Model integrity SHALL be continuously verified in production to detect unauthorized modification, replacement, or corruption. |
| BR-MDL-003 | The provenance of all third-party and open-source foundational models SHALL be verified before onboarding and periodically thereafter. |
| BR-MDL-004 | LLM deployments SHALL undergo automated testing for the OWASP LLM Top 10 vulnerability categories prior to production release. |
| BR-MDL-005 | Model risk assessments SHALL be documented and linked to the AI asset inventory, with findings tracked to remediation or risk acceptance. |
page_texts.20:
[strategy/white-papers/security/GUID-SEC-AI-SPM-REQS-v1.md#functional-requirements]

#### Functional Requirements

| ID | Requirement | Standards Alignment |
|---|---|---|
| FR-MDL-001 | The AI SPM tool SHALL provide or integrate with adversarial robustness evaluation frameworks (e.g., IBM Adversarial Robustness Toolbox, Microsoft Counterfit, or equivalent) to assess model susceptibility to evasion, poisoning, and model extraction attacks. | NIST AI RMF MEASURE 2.5; MITRE ATLAS TTP coverage |
| FR-MDL-002 | The tool SHALL generate and verify cryptographic hashes (SHA-256 or stronger) for model artifacts at rest and SHALL alert if model file integrity cannot be confirmed or if an artifact hash diverges from the registered baseline. | NIST SP 800-53 SI-7; IETF RFC 9334 (RATS) |
| FR-MDL-003 | The tool SHALL assess models for known backdoor patterns and anomalous behavior through behavioral testing at minimum on production deployment and after retraining events. | NIST AI RMF MEASURE 2.6; MITRE ATLAS AML.T0018 |
| FR-MDL-004 | For LLM-based systems, the tool SHALL perform automated prompt injection testing (direct and indirect), jailbreak resistance testing, and insecure output handling detection. | OWASP LLM01, LLM02, LLM05 (2025) |
| FR-MDL-005 | The tool SHALL evaluate model supply chain risk for third-party and open-source models, including provenance verification, license compliance, vulnerability advisories, and SBOM (Software Bill of Materials / AI Bill of Materials) integration. | NIST SP 800-218A PW.4; NIST SP 800-53 SA-12, SA-15 |
| FR-MDL-006 | The tool SHALL track model explainability posture — specifically whether deployed models have corresponding explainability mechanisms — and flag regulatory-scoped models (e.g., those making adverse benefit determinations) that lack documented explainability. | NIST AI 100-1 §2.6 |
| FR-MDL-007 | The tool SHALL provide a model risk score that aggregates adversarial robustness, integrity, supply chain, and explainability findings into a single, normalized risk indicator per model. | NIST AI RMF MEASURE 2.1 |

### Domain 4: AI Data Security and Privacy Posture

**Purpose:** Ensure that data used to train, validate, and operate AI systems is protected in accordance with classification requirements, privacy regulations, and data governance policies — covering training datasets, feature stores, inference inputs, and model outputs.

**Alignment:** NIST AI RMF MAP 2.3, MEASURE 2.10 | NIST SP 800-53 SC, MP, RA-3 | NIST SP 800-226 | HIPAA Security Rule
page_texts.22:
[strategy/white-papers/security/GUID-SEC-AI-SPM-REQS-v1.md#business-requirements]

#### Business Requirements

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| BR-DATA-001 | All training datasets used for AI systems SHALL be cataloged with data classification, source provenance, applicable privacy regulations (HIPAA, state privacy laws), and consent or data use agreement references. |
| BR-DATA-002 | Training datasets containing PHI, PII, or other regulated data SHALL be verified to have undergone approved de-identification or synthetic data generation prior to use. |
| BR-DATA-003 | Inference inputs and model outputs SHALL comply with data handling policies consistent with the sensitivity of the data being processed. |
| BR-DATA-004 | Data poisoning risks SHALL be assessed and controls verified for all training pipelines ingesting external or semi-trusted data sources. |
| BR-DATA-005 | AI data privacy posture SHALL be reportable to compliance and legal teams on demand with evidence suitable for regulatory audit response. |

| ID | Requirement | Standards Alignment |

| FR-DATA-005 | For LLM and RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) systems, the tool SHALL evaluate the security posture of connected knowledge bases and vector stores, including access controls, data classification of indexed content, and injection risk surface. | OWASP LLM06, LLM08 (2025); NIST AI RMF MEASURE 2.10 |

For systems already in production, non-adoption of these techniques SHOULD generate an advisory finding prompting engineering teams to assess feasibility. | NIST SP 800-226; NIST AI RMF MAP 2.3 |

### Domain 5: AI Supply Chain Security

**Purpose:** Manage risks arising from the AI software supply chain — including open-source model components, third-party AI APIs, AI-as-a-Service platforms, fine-tuning services, and dataset providers — through visibility, verification, and continuous monitoring.

**Alignment:** NIST AI RMF MAP 1.6, GOVERN 6.2 | NIST SP 800-53 SR, SA-12 | NIST SP 800-218A PW.4 | NIST CSF 2.0 GV.SC
page_texts.25:
[strategy/white-papers/security/GUID-SEC-AI-SPM-REQS-v1.md#business-requirements]

#### Business Requirements

| ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| BR-SCM-001 | The enterprise SHALL maintain a continuously updated AI Bill of Materials (AI-BOM) for every production AI system, covering model components, training libraries, inference runtimes, and third-party AI service dependencies. |
| BR-SCM-002 | Third-party AI models and AI-as-a-Service integrations SHALL undergo security and compliance review before onboarding. High-risk integrations SHALL complete a full security review including assessment of vendor security posture, data processing agreements, and AI governance practices. Moderate- and Low-risk integrations MAY satisfy this requirement through a lightweight self-assessment checklist approved by the security architecture team. |
| BR-SCM-003 | Known vulnerabilities in AI software supply chain components SHALL be tracked and remediated within risk-tiered SLAs. |
| BR-SCM-004 | The AI supply chain risk posture SHALL be reportable to executive leadership and auditors, demonstrating compliance with NIST SP 800-53 SR control family requirements. |
page_texts.26:
[strategy/white-papers/security/GUID-SEC-AI-SPM-REQS-v1.md#functional-requirements]

#### Functional Requirements

| ID | Requirement | Standards Alignment |

## 6. Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **AI SPM** | AI Security Posture Management — the discipline and supporting tooling for continuous security posture assessment, visibility, and governance across AI/ML systems |
| **AI-BOM** | AI Bill of Materials — a structured inventory of components that comprise an AI system, analogous to a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) but extended to include model artifacts, datasets, and AI-specific libraries |
| **Adversarial ML** | A category of attacks that exploit vulnerabilities specific to ML models, including evasion, poisoning, model inversion, model extraction, and backdoor attacks |
| **ATLAS** | MITRE ATLAS™ (Adversarial Threat Landscape for Artificial-Intelligence Systems) — a knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques |
| **CSPM** | Cloud Security Posture Management — tooling for continuous assessment of cloud infrastructure configuration against security baselines |
| **DSPM** | Data Security Posture Management — tooling for continuous discovery, classification, and security assessment of data across environments |
| **Model Drift** | Statistical divergence between a model's current input/output distributions and its baseline (training-time) distributions; security-relevant drift can indicate adversarial influence or poisoning |
| **Prompt Injection** | An attack class targeting LLMs in which adversarial instructions embedded in user input or retrieved context override system-defined behavior or extract privileged information |
| **RAG** | Retrieval-Augmented Generation — an LLM architecture pattern that supplements model responses with content retrieved from an external knowledge base at inference time |
| **RATS** | Remote ATtestation procedureS — IETF RFC 9334 architecture for hardware-backed integrity claims about software and firmware running on computing platforms |
